seriesTitle: The Lantern Mender of Pell Street
title: Two Cups

blocks.text: Black.
A hiss, like a wick catching. Rain on water, very close. And above the rain, a town clock that does not tick.
"One," Ada Brannock whispered. "Two. Three." Cold boards under her cheek. Sawdust. Lamp oil. "Four."
She opened her eyes. On the workbench above her sat a glass lantern, unlit, and over it, hanging in the air like a number on a meter, glowed one pale gold word.
WICK.
A fist hammered on the shop door. "Mender! Open up before I forget her!"
Ada got to her knees. The word hung there, steady as a pilot light. She shut her eyes, opened them again, and it was gone.
Head injury, she told herself. Visual disturbance. Get up. Find out where you are. Get home.
The last thing she remembered was a hospital going dark around her, and a generator coming up too slowly. After that, nothing. Then boards.
The fist again. "Mender!"
She found the door by the sound of it. A narrow shop: shelves of brass cages and empty glass, a bench under the window, rain sliding down the panes. She drew the bolt.

On the step stood a big man in a wet oilskin, grey beard, grey eyebrows, both arms wrapped around a lantern as if it were a sleeping child. The glass had a crack running through it, fine as a hair. The flame inside stuttered.
"About time," he said. "Light came on in here. Saw it from the tower. So you're the new one. Mend it."
"I'm not anybody's anything," Ada said. "Where is this? What town?"
"Morrow Quay. Pell Street. Half past too late, that's where." He pushed the lantern at her. "Mend it."
"Sorry," she said, and meant it, and went past him into the rain.
The street ran downhill to a market, and the market was lit.

Lamps on poles. Lamps hung from the stall awnings. Fog rolling between them so thick that every stall was its own small room of yellow light, and between the rooms, nothing. She could hear water slapping stone somewhere below, and oars, and fat spitting in a pan, and a hundred people talking at once.
Nobody had a car. Nobody had a phone out. She checked her own. Dead. It had been dead since she woke.
"Come on, you useless thing," she told it, and put it away.
A man was roasting chestnuts over a brazier, and he had a kind enough face, so she asked him. "The road out. Which way? Bus, train, I'll walk if I have to."
He looked at her for a long moment. "The fog road?"
"Any road."

"There's only the one, and it's shut." He nodded uphill, past the roofs, to where a clock tower stood black against the fog. Its face was lit by nothing. Its hands were still. "Shut ten years. Since the clock stopped. Nobody's gone out and nobody's come in." He turned a chestnut with bare fingers, not flinching at the heat. "Till tonight, maybe. You came out of the mender's shop. I saw the light."
Ada opened her mouth to tell him she was an electrician from a hospital a very long way from here, and found the words would not fit in this air. They sounded like a story.
From the next stall, lost in the fog, a woman laughed.

"Two of everything!" The voice was quick and bright and went everywhere at once. "Two loaves, two lemons, two of those little cakes with the pink on top, and I live on my own! And this morning, you'll love this, I set out two cups. Two. Poured both. Sat there talking to the steam like it was going to answer me back."
"Again?" the chestnut man called.
"Again, and you're going to say I'm going soft, I know, I know." The laugh came again, softer at the end. "No idea why. Not the faintest."
Ada stepped toward the voice. The fog shifted, and there was only a green umbrella going away between the lamps, and someone a few stalls down humming as they worked, and then nothing.
A bell rang out, deep and slow, from somewhere across the water.
"Ninth bell," said the chestnut man. "Lamps up. You'd best get back to your shop, Mender. He'll still be waiting."
Ada walked the other way.

She walked until the market lamps ran out, and the cobbles ran out, and there was only a pale road going up into a wall of fog. She walked into it, counting her steps. At twelve she couldn't see her hands. At twenty the cold was in her teeth, and the only sound in the world was her own breath, and somewhere behind her, the clock not ticking.
She counted back down to zero, walking backward, and came out shaking.
He was still on the step.

Rain dripped from the brim of his cap and the end of his nose. The lantern was inside his coat now, held against his chest. He was tapping the brass cage with one finger, a steady little rhythm. Tick. Tick-tick. Tick.
"Told you," he said. "Half past too late."
"Who are you?"

"Tobias Penhallow. Clocks." He tilted his head at the tower. "That clock. Her. Ten years I've been putting her back together, and I'm one wheel from done, and it's going." He tapped his temple, hard. "The train of her. Third wheel to fourth. Had it this morning. Gone by dinner. By tomorrow I'll be standing up that tower holding a gear like a man holding a stranger's hat."
"I'm an electrician," Ada said. "I fix wiring. I don't know what a mender is."
"Don't need to know. Need to do." He held the lantern out to her in the rain. "Please."
He said it as if it cost him something. She suspected it did.
She took it. She meant to hand it straight back.
The word bloomed over the glass.
WICK, in pale gold. Under it, a thin line of light traced the crack exactly, every branch of it, and beside that sat a bar, empty, waiting. It was a readout. There was no other word for it.
Ada stood very still in the doorway.
Twelve years on the tools. You do not trust a thing because it looks dead. You do not trust a thing because it looks live. You test before you touch.
"Inside," she said. "Stand back from the bench. Hands in your pockets."
Tobias grumbled something about being ordered about on his own street, and did exactly as he was told.

She set the lantern on the bench. She held one finger a hair's breadth from the crack, not touching, and the bar on the readout flickered, the way a tester flickers near a live wire. She moved her finger along. The flicker followed. A fault, then. That was all it was. A break in a line, and on either side of it, the current wanting to get through.
"Right," Ada said quietly. "Right. I can do a fault."
She touched the glass.

It was warm, warmer than the little flame could make it. The wick hissed. Under her fingertip the glass clicked, a tiny sound, like a cooling kettle. The bar on the readout began to fill. She followed the crack the way she'd follow a cable through a wall, slow and patient, and wherever she had been, the line of light went out and the glass behind it was whole.
She was counting under her breath. She didn't notice she was doing it.
Halfway along, the shop went away.
Water to the knees, and rising. Cold enough to stop a heart.

Night, and no lamps. That was the first thing she understood. A long stone quay, every lamp along it dark, and the only light coming from somewhere far up the hill. People shouting. Someone screaming a name she couldn't catch. The canal was not a canal any more. It was climbing the steps like something alive.
She was looking out through someone else's eyes. Big hands in front of her, younger than the ones on Pell Street, but the same hands. Tobias's hands.
Overhead, something cracked. A long, splitting sound, timber tearing along the grain, loud as a mast going over.

A woman stood just ahead on the flooded stones, half turned away. Small. Dark hair plastered flat with rain. She turned at the sound, and Ada saw her face in the light from up the hill: a wide mouth, a dimple in one cheek, eyes gone huge.
Tobias's hands went out and struck her square between the shoulders.
She went backward off the quay into the black water, and the water closed over her, and she did not come up.
Someone was breathing in great sobbing pulls. Tobias, young. Whispering it into the dark, over and over, like a man winding a spring.
"I did it. God forgive me. I did it."
Ada was on the floor. She didn't remember falling.

The bench was above her. The lantern sat on it, whole. Not a mark on the glass. The flame stood up straight and steady, and the readout over it showed the bar full, then faded like a screen going to sleep.
Tobias was kneeling beside her, one hand held out, not quite touching her shoulder.

"Third wheel to fourth," he said. "Sixty-four teeth, pinion of eight. Fourth to the escape wheel, sixty, pinion of eight." His voice was rough. He was tapping on the floorboards. Tick. Tick-tick. Tick. "It's all there. Every tooth."
Ada sat up. Her mouth tasted of canal. "Who was she?"
The tapping stopped.
"Who?"
"The woman on the quay. In the water." Ada swallowed. "I saw it. I don't know how, but I saw it."
Tobias got slowly to his feet. He picked up the lantern and held it the way he had on the step, close against his chest.
"So it shows you," he said. "Thought it might."
"Who was she?"

"Don't know." He said it to the window, not to her. "I know what I did. I know her face. Every night, I know her face. Her name—" His finger found the bench and tapped once, and stopped. "I'd swear I had it once. Gone. Like a wheel out of the train." He pulled his cap down. "That's all you're getting."
"Mr Penhallow—"

"Kettle's on the hob," he said at the door, gruff as a hinge. "Use it. You look like half past dead." He set a coin on the bench without looking at it, and went out into the rain, and she heard him tap the doorframe once on his way.
The kettle was where he'd said. Ada made tea in a chipped cup and stood holding it, not drinking.

A man had pushed a woman into the water and could not say who she was. A whole town had a road it couldn't use and a clock that didn't run. A voice in the fog had set out two cups and couldn't say why.
She did what she always did when a day went this wrong. She took out her phone to ring her mum.

Dead, of course. Still dead. "Fine," she muttered. "Fine. I'll do it from memory, soon as I find a phone that works." And she began to say the number over to herself, the way you say a thing to keep it safe.
The first four digits came. Then nothing.
Not a blur. Not a half-remembered shape. A clean gap, like a cut cable.

She tested it the way she'd test any fault. Start at the source. Go slow. She counted the digits off on her fingers. Four. She had four. She'd known that number longer than she'd known her own. She went back to the top and tried again, slower. Four. Again. Four, and then the line went dead.
She put the cup down very carefully, so it wouldn't rattle.

Then she found a pencil in the bench drawer and a sheet of brown wrapping paper, smoothed it flat, and wrote across the top in capitals, the way she'd label a fuse board so the next person through wouldn't get hurt.
THINGS I'VE LOST.
Underneath, smaller: Mum's phone number.
She looked at it for a long time.
Then she pulled the big ledger from the end of the bench and opened it, to find out what she had signed up for.
The first page was written in a hand that slanted hard to the right, as if it were late for something. Heavy underlining. No name.
RULES. FOR WHOEVER COMES NEXT.
Ada read it aloud, because the shop was too quiet.
"One. Every mend costs you a memory. One. Yours." Yours was underlined three times. "You don't choose it. If you did, I'd have got rid of long division."
"Two. Write down what goes. You won't feel it leave, so you won't know otherwise. That's the trick of it."
"Three. Read rule two again."
"Four. Believe the light over the glass before you believe the customer. The light doesn't want anything from you."
There were more rules, pages of them, and margin notes crowding every edge like people at a rail.
Ada looked from rule two to the brown paper beside her, where she had already done it without being told.
"Bloody thing," she said to the ledger, and went on reading until the lamp burned low and her cheek came down on the page.
A bell woke her. Not the deep one from across the water. A small, bright, tinny one, right over her head.
The shop bell. Grey light in the window. The rain had stopped.

"Morning! Oh, you're open. Are you open? You look open." Quick footsteps on the boards, and the shake of a wet umbrella. "Whole street's saying there's a new mender, and I said, well, that's lucky, because I've got something wants mending, haven't I, and I'm not one to wait about—"
Ada lifted her head from the ledger.

The woman in the doorway was small, with dark hair pinned up and coming down. She was shaking out a green umbrella. She had a wide mouth, and a dimple in one cheek, and she was pink with cold, and alive, and talking.
It was the voice from the market. The woman who set out two cups.
And it was the face Ada had watched go under the black water last night, and not come up.
